01 — Project Overview

From a flat log file to an automated response pipeline

This project simulates the first duties of a SOC analyst: spotting malicious authentication activity in logs, then scaling that detection into a SIEM and automating the response. It progresses in four real, verified phases — nothing here is theoretical; every log line, error message and screenshot in this report came from an actual run.

🔎 Detect

Native grep/awk analysis, then the same logic reproduced in Splunk SPL for scale.

⚔️ Validate

A real Hydra dictionary attack against a lab SSH service, not simulated data.

🧪 Enrich

Two independent reputation sources (AbuseIPDB, VirusTotal) cross-check every flagged IP.

🧑‍💻 Decide

A conditional branch filters noise; a human analyst reviews before anything irreversible happens.

02 — Phase 1

Linux-native log analysis (grep / awk)

Starting point: a simulated auth.log for a small web server, analyzed with nothing but core Linux utilities — the baseline every SOC analyst should be able to do before reaching for a SIEM.

grep 'sshd' syslog
grep 'Jun 12' syslog | grep 'sshd'

The parsing gotcha

A naive awk '{print $11}' extraction silently grabbed the wrong column whenever sshd logged an invalid user attempt, because that message format inserts two extra words and shifts every fixed-position field. The fix: a conditional column selection based on message shape.

awk '/sshd/ && /Failed password/ {
  if ($0 ~ /invalid user/) print $13; else print $11
}' auth.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
IndicatorValueVerdict
Brute-force source203.0.113.778 failed root/admin attempts → block/alert
Enumeration source198.51.100.234 attempts on non-existent users → block/alert
Legitimate access192.168.1.0/245 internal, known-user logins → no action
03 — Phase 2

Live attack lab — Hydra against a real SSH service

To validate the methodology on a real system (not just sample files), a Kali VM ran a Hydra dictionary attack against its own local SSH service, with explicit written scope: lab-owned, isolated, NAT-only.

hydra -l kali -P ~/soc-lab/passwords.txt -t 4 ssh://127.0.0.1
# [22][ssh] host: 127.0.0.1  login: kali  password: kali
Gotcha — modern Kali ships no /var/log/auth.log; auth events live in the systemd journal under sshd-session (OpenSSH ≥ 9.8 split the daemon), not sshd. The classic journalctl _COMM=sshd filter returns nothing useful.
04 — Phase 3

Scaling detection into Splunk Enterprise

The same brute-force logic from the awk scripts was rebuilt as a proper SPL search, then wired into a scheduled, webhook-triggering alert.

index=main sourcetype=linux_secure "Failed password"
| rex field=_raw "from (?<src_ip>\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)"
| stats count by src_ip
| where count > 5
05 — Phase 4

SOAR automation with Shuffle

The Splunk alert's webhook feeds a Shuffle workflow that enriches the flagged IP against two independent reputation sources, branches on confidence, and reports a response — without ever executing an irreversible action automatically.

Step 1 — AbuseIPDB enrichment

GET https://api.abuseipdb.com/api/v2/check?ipAddress=$exec.result.src_ip
Headers: Key: <api_key>, Accept: application/json

Step 2 — Conditional branch

Three outgoing edges from the AbuseIPDB node are each gated by a condition on $http_1.body.data.abuseConfidenceScore, so downstream nodes only fire for sufficiently confident results.

Step 3 — VirusTotal cross-check

GET https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/ip_addresses/$exec.result.src_ip
Headers: x-apikey: <api_key>, Accept: application/json

Step 4 — Analyst notification

Step 5 — Dry-run firewall simulation

Rather than executing a real iptables block, a firewall-sim Http POST node sends a structured dry-run report to a Discord webhook — remediation stays observable and reversible instead of live and irreversible.

Conditional branch

abuseConfidenceScore > 50 gates which IPs reach the analyst and the firewall simulation — keeping low-confidence noise out.

Cross-validation

VirusTotal's last_analysis_stats.malicious, country, AS owner and tags corroborate the AbuseIPDB score before any action.

Human-in-the-loop

An email notifies the analyst with full context; nothing destructive fires without review.

Dry-run remediation

A simulated firewall action is posted to Discord — observable and reversible, not a live iptables block.

06 — Troubleshooting

Real problems hit (and fixed) along the way

In the spirit of honest documentation, here's what actually broke during setup — these are the moments that build real operational skill, not the parts that worked on the first try.

Disk space blocked Splunk. The swap partition sat between root and free disk space, blocking growpart. Fixed by deleting the swap partition, extending root (growpart + resize2fs), and recreating swap as a file instead.
Self-hosted Shuffle failed to dispatch workers. network shuffle_swarm_executions not found, then a Swarm advertise-address error — caused by the lab VM having two active NICs (NAT + host-only), confusing Orborus's auto-detection. Resolved with docker swarm init --advertise-addr <eth0 IP>, then ultimately moved to Shuffle's managed cloud to stay focused on the SOC logic rather than container orchestration.
JSON body broke on a list-type variable. The Discord dry-run message failed with SyntaxError - invalid syntax. Perhaps you forgot a comma? — a VirusTotal tags field (a list) was inserted as raw text into a hand-built JSON string. Fixed by scoping the body to scalar fields first, validating, then reintroducing list fields carefully.
API key hygiene. The AbuseIPDB key was briefly visible in plaintext during live troubleshooting screenshots and was regenerated immediately afterward as a precaution. A reminder that screenshots meant for documentation should have secrets redacted before capture, not after.
